title: Redwood discovery - Sierra Bank latency & throughput
summary: Intro discovery call focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency requirements, and benchmarking approach across Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer concerned about streaming for real-time chat, p95 SLA ~200-300ms for short prompts, and peak concurrency of ~600 concurrent users. Agreed next steps: share benchmarking plan, security deck, pricing for dedicated pool, and schedule a pilot benchmark run in two weeks.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
action_items: Maya Chen: Send Redwood dedicated pricing and burst policy (due 2026-03-06)
Diego Alvarez: Draft benchmark plan and test harness (due 2026-03-10)
Laura Kim: Share sample prompt corpus and SLA requirements (due 2026-03-09)
next_steps: Redwood to share security/compliance deck and SOC2 snapshot
Schedule pilot benchmark: Redwood runs 100k tokens synthetic test + customer prompts
Follow-up call to review benchmark results and capacity sizing (target 2026-03-18)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE. Diego from our SE team is with me. quick intros?
[00:10] Laura Kim: Laura here, head of ML at Sierra Bank. Raj's infra, and Emma PM. We've been evaluating hosted vs private given compliance requirements.
[00:25] Diego Alvarez: great, thanks. high level — are you mainly concerned about latency p95 or throughput first?
[00:30] Laura Kim: p95 is the big one. For our fraud chat feature, we want p95 under 300ms for ~30 token responses, ideally ~200ms. Concurrency — estimated 600 concurrent chat sessions at peak, but average is 120. Streaming is required; we need partial tokens to appear quickly.
[00:50] Raj Patel: also data residency and audit logs. We need keys in our KMS if you do private. SOC 2 is a must.
[01:02] Maya Chen: totally, we support SOC 2, KMS integrations, VPC/private deployment. For latency, Hosted is usually fastest to stand up but Dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools and predictable throughput. Private gives max control but adds ops.
[01:20] Emma Stone: what's the difference in p95 numbers between Hosted and Dedicated in your benchmarks?
[01:26] Diego Alvarez: depends on model and request pattern. For short prompts (<=50 tokens) on our hosted API with our optimized kernels we often see p95 ~120-220ms for 8k context models under low contention. Dedicated with reserved capacity reduces jitter — p95 can be 90-180ms because we avoid noisy neighbors and can tune batching. Private similar to Dedicated but added network overhead in customer's VPC can add 20-60ms if cross-region.
[01:54] Laura Kim: okay, and what about token/sec? We need to sustain bursts of ~1.5k tokens/sec across the fleet, and per-request throughput matters for streaming.
[02:05] Diego Alvarez: we measure both tokens/sec and tokens/sec per-GPU. Example: an A100-ish pod with our runtime can push ~800-1200 tokens/sec for 8k models with quantization and batching. For streaming we optimize prefix caching to lower per-token compute. 
[02:25] Raj Patel: our infra team is worried about concurrency and autoscaling cold-starts. If you spike from 120 to 600 concurrent users how do you handle it?
[02:35] Maya Chen: we have autoscale policies and burst capacity for Dedicated; Hosted has dynamic scaling with regional pools and graceful fallbacks to smaller models if capacity constrained. We can set warm pools to reduce cold-start tail latencies.
[02:50] Emma Stone: any real customers with sub-200ms p95?
[02:54] Diego Alvarez: yes — a payments client with small prompt sizes achieved 180ms p95 on Dedicated with 2x reserved A100s and aggressive batching disabled for low-latency. There's always a tradeoff: batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency.
[03:12] Laura Kim: about benchmarking — can you run our prompt corpus? We need representative results not synthetic.
[03:18] Maya Chen: absolutely. action here: Diego will draft a benchmark plan to run both synthetic token/sec and your prompts, across Hosted & Dedicated. We'll instrument latency histograms, p50/p95/p99, and streaming time-to-first-byte.
[03:34] Raj Patel: what telemetry do we get? Trace-level timings? token breakdown?
[03:38] Diego Alvarez: yes — per-request token timing, KV cache hit rates, batching sizes, and per-token compute time. Redwood Console shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns.
[03:50] Laura Kim: on security, send the SOC2 and a summary for KMS integration and whether keys ever leave our control.
[03:58] Maya Chen: we'll share the security deck. for Private, keys stay in your KMS; we support bring-your-own-key and HSM integrations.
[04:06] Emma Stone: timelines — we want a pilot in March and production by end of Q2. Is that realistic?
[04:12] Diego Alvarez: yes, pilot (benchmarks + 2-week sample) in March is realistic. Production depends on Dedicated provisioning time — usually a couple of weeks once commit is signed.
[04:22] Laura Kim: what about fallback policies? If Dedicated hits capacity do you route to Hosted? We can't send PII out.
[04:30] Maya Chen: routing policies are policy-driven. For data-sensitive routes you can pin to Private or Dedicated; fallback can be disabled for those routes. We can also anonymize or strip PII before routing.
[04:40] Raj Patel: pricing sensitivity — what's incremental cost to reserve burst capacity?
[04:44] Maya Chen: we'll send targeted pricing. generally reserved capacity has lower unit cost; burst is an add-on that charges for buffer capacity. We'll include examples in the pricing doc.
[04:56] Emma Stone: for streaming, do you support partial result tokens over websockets?
[05:00] Diego Alvarez: yes, streaming via websocket or SSE and function/tool calling is supported. Time-to-first-token is a key metric we'll capture.
[05:10] Laura Kim: curious — you mentioned KV cache and prefix caching. For chat we do a lot of session history. Does Redwood cache per conversation?
[05:18] Diego Alvarez: yes, we do KV cache for transformer key/values and optional prefix cache for frequently used prompts; can be shared across requests to reduce compute. Cache hit rate directly reduces tokens/sec load and improves latency.
[05:30] Maya Chen: can you walk through a sample SLA?
[05:33] Emma Stone: (laughs) sure we can, but...
[05:35] Laura Kim: main targets are p95 <= 300ms for short replies, p99 < 800ms, and sustainable fleet token throughput > 1.5k tokens/sec during peaks.
[05:50] Diego Alvarez: noted. we'll include a benchmark scenario that targets those numbers and show failure modes.
[05:58] Raj Patel: about network — if we run Private in our VPC, what's the expected additional latency?
[06:05] Diego Alvarez: usually 10-40ms depending on region and routing. We'll run a test with your VPC to quantify.
[06:12] Laura Kim: any caveats for quantized models? We want accuracy preserved.
[06:17] Diego Alvarez: quantization can change latency/throughput positively with small quality tradeoffs. Redwood Optimize recommends quant profiles based on your evals. We'll recommend several profiles and show quality deltas on your prompt set.
[06:30] Emma Stone: stakeholders — who's involved from our side besides ML/Infra/PM? Legal for contracts, security team for SOC2 review.
[06:38] Maya Chen: our enterprise sales and security will engage. Next steps: security deck, pricing, benchmark plan, and scheduling the pilot.
[06:45] Laura Kim: great. thanks.
[06:47] Maya Chen: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and propose dates.
[06:52] (call ends)

Note: transcript has occasional transcription errors and speaker attribution approximated, timestamps approximate.
